content: The quality of the evidence was thoroughly evaluated to determine the direction and strength of the recommendations. This process involved several steps, including the establishment of a Guidelines Development Group and the formulation of specific questions within the framework of screening, care, and treatment. These questions were structured using the PICO format (Population, Intervention, Comparison, Outcomes). Systematic reviews of the best available evidence were conducted, and the findings were assessed for quality and presented in GRADE evidence profiles. Additionally, existing national and international guidelines were reviewed, and comprehensive reviews and technical reports were obtained when necessary. The final recommendations were reached by consensus during a meeting of the Guidelines Development Group in June 2013. By the time of the June 2013 meeting, it was anticipated that two additional medications, simeprevir and sofosbuvir, would likely be approved in at least one country (the United States) before the release of these guidelines. Consequently, recommendations for their use were included. Using the same methodology applied to all recommendations in these guidelines, additional systematic reviews were commissioned, and evidence profiles and decision-making tables were prepared. These were reviewed by the Guidelines Development Group during a web-based meeting in December 2013, leading to the development of recommendations for the use of simeprevir and sofosbuvir. The final version of the document was subsequently approved by the WHO Guidelines Review Committee. Recommendations on Screening for HCV Infection: 1. Screening to Identify Individuals with HCV Infection: It is recommended that HCV serology testing be offered to individuals who belong to populations with a high prevalence of HCV or who have a history of HCV risk exposure or behavior. This is a strong recommendation based on moderate-quality evidence. 2. Confirmation of Chronic HCV Infection: It is suggested that nucleic acid testing (NAT) for HCV RNA be performed immediately following a positive HCV serological test to confirm the diagnosis of chronic HCV infection. NAT for HCV RNA should also be part of the assessment for initiating treatment. This is a conditional recommendation based on very low-quality evidence. Recommendations on the Care of People Infected with HCV: 3. Screening for Alcohol Use and Counseling: An assessment of alcohol intake is recommended for all individuals with HCV infection. Behavioral interventions to reduce alcohol consumption should be offered to those with moderate-to-high alcohol intake. This is a strong recommendation based on moderate-quality evidence. 4. Assessment of Liver Fibrosis and Cirrhosis: In resource-limited settings, it is suggested that the aminotransferase/platelet ratio index (APRI) or FIB-4 tests be used to assess hepatic fibrosis rather than more resource-intensive tests such as elastography or FibroTest. This is a conditional recommendation based on low-quality evidence. Recommendations on the Treatment of HCV Infection: 5. Assessment for HCV Treatment: All adults and children with chronic HCV infection, including people who inject drugs, should be assessed for antiviral treatment. This is a strong recommendation based on moderate-quality evidence. 6. Treatment with Pegylated Interferon and Ribavirin: Pegylated interferon in combination with ribavirin is recommended for the treatment of chronic HCV infection rather than standard non-pegylated interferon with ribavirin. This is a strong recommendation based on moderate-quality evidence. 7. Treatment with Telaprevir or Boceprevir: For individuals with genotype 1 chronic HCV infection, treatment with direct-acting antivirals (telaprevir or boceprevir) in combination with pegylated interferon and ribavirin is suggested rather than pegylated interferon and ribavirin alone. This is a conditional recommendation based on moderate-quality evidence. 8. Treatment with Sofosbuvir: Sofosbuvir, in combination with ribavirin with or without pegylated interferon (depending on the HCV genotype), is recommended for genotypes 1, 2, 3, and 4 HCV infection rather than pegylated interferon and ribavirin alone. This is a strong recommendation based on high-quality evidence. 9. Treatment with Simeprevir: Simeprevir, in combination with pegylated interferon and ribavirin, is recommended for individuals with genotype 1b HCV infection and for those with genotype 1a HCV infection without the Q80K polymorphism, rather than pegylated interferon and ribavirin alone. This is a strong recommendation based on high-quality evidence. Note: Recommendations 8 and 9 were made without considering resource use, as pricing information was unavailable for most countries at the time of formulation. HCV Screening: Screening for HCV infection involves an initial serologic test followed by an HCV RNA test (quantitative or qualitative) to confirm viremia and chronic infection. Approximately 15–45% of individuals initially infected will spontaneously clear the virus, typically within six months of infection. Those who do not clear the virus within this timeframe are classified as having chronic HCV infection. Screening is particularly important for individuals at risk, such as those undergoing medical procedures in settings with poor infection control, people who inject drugs, and individuals exposed to contaminated equipment. Sexual partners of HCV-infected individuals are at low risk, but higher-risk groups include HIV-infected men who have sex with men and infants born to HCV-infected mothers. WHO recommends HCV serology testing for individuals in high-prevalence populations or with a history of risk exposure, rather than waiting for symptomatic disease presentation. Care of Patients with HCV: HCV-related liver disease, such as cirrhosis, can take decades to develop. During this time, clinicians should monitor and manage hepatic diseases from other causes and address extrahepatic manifestations of HCV, such as insulin resistance and diabetes. Addressing co-morbidities like high BMI and smoking is also critical. Alcohol use, which accelerates HCV-related cirrhosis progression, should be assessed, and behavioral interventions should be offered to reduce intake. WHO recommends using the ASSIST framework for alcohol screening and reduction interventions, which is evidence-based and designed for primary healthcare settings. Assessment of Liver Fibrosis: Deciding when to initiate HCV therapy requires reliable assessment of liver fibrosis. While liver biopsy was historically the gold standard, it is expensive, carries risks, and requires expert interpretation. Non-invasive tests, such as APRI and FIB-4, are more suitable for resource-limited settings. Transient elastography, though effective, is costly and less accessible. Patients with advanced fibrosis (METAVIR stages F3 and F4) should be prioritized for treatment due to their higher risk of cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma. If resources allow, individuals with less advanced fibrosis (METAVIR stages F1 and F2) may also be considered for treatment. Treatment of Hepatitis C: The high cost of treatment, the need for sophisticated laboratory monitoring, and the adverse effects of existing medications (interferon and ribavirin) have limited access to HCV treatment, particularly in lowand middle-income countries. Even in high-income countries, treatment is often denied to certain groups, such as current or former drug users. WHO recommends that all adults and children with chronic HCV infection, including people who inject drugs, be assessed for treatment. Pegylated interferon with ribavirin is superior to standard interferon with ribavirin and is recommended for treating chronic HCV infection. For genotype 1 HCV infection, direct-acting antivirals (telaprevir, boceprevir, or simeprevir) in combination with pegylated interferon and ribavirin are recommended over pegylated interferon and ribavirin alone. Sofosbuvir, in combination with ribavirin or pegylated interferon/ribavirin, is recommended for genotypes 1–4.
